speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like also at this time to make a statement on the government's policy on bilingualism in the public service. I hope the house will agree that the importance of this subject justifies the fact that the statement is a little longer than would normally be acceptable.
It is the objective of the government to make the public service of maximum benefit to the people of Canada by attracting to it
the most competent and qualified Canadians available in all parts of Canada. To this end, and having regard to the character of our country, the government for several years has been taking practical steps to encourage bilingualism in the federal public service as part of its fundamental objective of promoting and strengthening national unity on the basis of the equality of rights and opportunities for both English speaking and French speaking Canadians.
In a diverse federal state such as Canada it is important that all citizens should have a fair and equal opportunity to participate in the national administration and to identify themselves with, and feel at home in, their own national capital. The government hopes and expects that, within a reasonable period of years, a state of affairs in the public service will be reached whereby
(a)	it will be normal practice for oral or written communications within the service to be made in either official language at the option of the person making them, in the knowledge that they will be understood by those directly concerned;
(b)	communications with the public will normally be in either official language having regard to the person being served;
(c)	the linguistic and cultural values of both English speaking and French speaking Canadians will be reflected through civil service recruitment and training; and
(d)	a climate will be created in which public servants from both language groups will work together toward common goals, using their own language and applying their respective cultural values, but each fully understanding and appreciating those of the other.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
In developing measures to assist those now in the public service more effectively to achieve a reasonable proficiency in both official languages and to improve the recruitment of civil servants with this proficiency, the government has been guided by the following principles:
(a)	The achievement of bilingualism is in itself a desirable objective for any Canadian citizen. Where the need for bilingualism clearly exists in practice, above all in the
3916	COMMONS
Bilingualism in Public Service national capital, it should be recognized as an element of merit in selection for civil service positions.
(b)	In conformity with the merit system, which must remain unimpaired, the requirement for bilingualism should relate to positions, and not only to individuals.
(c)	Bilingualism must be introduced gradually over a period of years in a manner which will not lead to injustice or misunderstanding. The various measures should be integrated into a well defined, long term program.
(d)	It must therefore be a requirement of any program that, in areas where a need for bilingualism exists, civil servants and prospective recruits must be provided with adequate time and opportunity to adapt themselves to new conditions in the service in a way that will increase their own possibilities for a successful and satisfying career.
(e)	For similar reasons of equity, the careers of civil servants who are not bilingual and who have devoted many years of their lives to the service of their country must not be prejudiced in any way by measures to develop bilingualism.
(f)	The government will consult from time to time with civil service associations concerning its policy on bilingualism in order to obtain their point of view, and to provide them with all reasonable assurances and remove any possible misunderstandings in regard to measures being proposed.
On the basis of the above objectives of policy and principles of action the government has approved the following measures:
I. In respect of civil service positions
requiring prior university training
1. (a) Beginning in 1967, reasonable proficiency in the two official languages or willingness to acquire it within a prescribed period of time through appropriate training at public expense will be an element of merit in the selection of university graduates recruited for administrative trainee positions where the need for bilingualism exists, as is already being done in the case of candidates for foreign service positions.
(b) In those centres where a need exists for reasonable proficiency in both languages, procedures will progressively be established for the filling of executive and administrative positions, so that by about 1970 in the case of appointments from outside the service and by about 1975 in the case of promotions from within, bilingual proficiency or willingness to acquire it will normally be a requirement for

DEBATES	April 6, 1966
the positions in such centres; that is, where a need exists for reasonable proficiency in both languages.
(c) These procedures will not cover at this time the technical, professional and scientific positions in the civil service, the armed forces or federal crown agencies as these categories present special problems. The appropriate departmental and agency authorities are therefore being asked to submit a long term program of effective action in their respective areas of responsibility which takes these special problems and particular difficulties into account.
2. A special pool of positions will be established in the national capital to be used to facilitate the recruitment and to accelerate the development of candidates of high potential who are proficient in both languages.
II. In respect of senior executive officers
A special program for improving bilingualism among senior executive officers serving in the national capital will be undertaken. It is envisaged that each year some 20 English speaking civil servants from the most senior categories, plus their families, will spend a 12 month period in a mainly French speaking city, while some 10 French speaking civil servants and their families will spend a similar period in a mainly English speaking city, to study the other official language and gain an understanding of the cultural values of the group they are visiting.
In respect of bilingual clerical and secretarial positions, it has been agreed in principle that a higher rate of pay will be paid in future in respect of clerical and secretarial positions in which there is the requirement for a knowledge of both languages and where both are used in the performance of duties, providing the incumbents of such positions meet standards of competence established by the Civil Service Commission.
The present program of language training will be strengthened and expanded to make the most effective contribution to the development of proficiency in both languages in the public service in those centres where the need for such proficiency exists.
The federal government will undertake discussions with the Ontario and Quebec governments concerning the early establishment of a secondary school in the Ottawa area in which the language of instruction will be French, in order to meet the requirements of those who wish to provide their children with
April 6. 1966

secondary education in French, and concerning other joint measures that would directly or indirectly contribute to the improvement of the bicultural character of the civil service in the national capital.
A special secretariat on bilingualism is being established within the privy council office under my direction. Working in close consultation and co-operation with the Civil Service Commission, the Treasury Board and all deputy ministers and heads of agencies, it will be responsible for ensuring the coordinated and progressive implementation of the government's policy and program regarding bilingualism in the public service.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express the sincere hope that on the eve of our centennial, all Canadians will share my deep conviction that the policy and program of the government on bilingualism in the public service will be to make a very important, indeed an essential, contribution to the promotion of national unity and to a great and stronger Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say at once that any action to promote the objective set out in the concluding paragraph of the Prime Minister's speech will, I know, receive the fullest support from this group. Our record during the period we were in office was one of continuing steps forward toward the assurance of full partnership of those of English and French origin in building Canada, without in any way diminishing the rights of those millions from other racial origins.
During our period of office we, for the first time in Canada's history, made the House of Commons bilingual in fact. When I first entered the House of Commons anyone speaking in the French language received even less attention than those of us who spoke in English. Indeed, when a person spoke in the French language the house emptied because so many of the members were unable to follow what was being said. We brought in simultaneous interpretation.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
During our period of office we brought about the opportunity for those of French language to have a larger share in high positions of government, something they had not had before. We made provision for the appointment of ambassadors of French language and French origin so that in all parts of the world the character of this country would be made clear.
Bilingualism in Public Service
I mention these things as evidence of our attitude. Indeed, it was under our administration that for the first time there was any recognition of French speaking countries in Africa for assistance from Canada, to the end that in a spirit of co-operation we would thereby epitomize something of the relationship which we have under our constitution. In addition, it was under our administration that Her Majesty's representative in Canada, the Governor General, for the first time since Vaudreuil became a Canadian of French origin. I mention these things merely for the purpose of assuring that the record is clear and not subject to the kind of misinterpretation which it sometimes suffers.
The constitutional rights provided for under the British North America Act, in the opinion of the Conservative party, are inviolable, and cannot be changed except by unanimity. We took the stand in 1946 when Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent was Prime Minister of Canada. When he as a constitutional lawyer expressed the view that the rights of language and education enshrined in sections 91 and 92 could be altered by a simple majority of parliament we said no, that could not be done.
He never said any such thing.

That was our stand. That was our attitude, and that attitude still prevails. Indeed, I can do no better than quote Sir John A. Macdonald when, within a year from his death, he expressed what has been the viewpoint of the Conservative party throughout the years. These were his words:
I have no accord with the desire expressed in some quarters that, by any mode whatever, there should be an attempt made to oppress the one language or to render it inferior to the other. I believe that would be impossible if it were tried, and it would be foolish and wicked if it were possible.
That, Mr. Speaker, has represented our view. Now, at a time when the report of the B and B commission, which has been spoken of in such fulsome terms by members of the government, has not yet been presented, we come to deal, not through parliament but through governmental action, with a major element in the whole field of bilingualism. Under section 133 of the British North America Act use of the English and French languages on an equal basis was recognized in parliament, in the Quebec legislature, in federal courts and in the courts of Quebec. There is also authorization for the publication of federal legislation and legislation in
April 6, 1966

Bilingualism in Public Service Quebec in both languages. These are sacred rights.
Sir, there are divisions within our country. There always have been. The Prime Minister hopes that on the eve of our hundredth year of confederation we shall be able to do something to solve those difficulties. We took the stand that in an equal partnership, constitutional rights should be maintained based on mutual respect and recognition. Speaking in February, 1963 on behalf of the government I used these words:
There have, however, arisen from time to time, questions as to whether Canada, as she approaches the first century of Confederation, has achieved the full measure of the vision of the Fathers of Confederation.
I suggested, with of course the unanimous support of the cabinet and our colleagues in the House of Commons, that there should be convened a national confederation conference, which would deal with certain matters, including those now being dealt with in this rather uncertain, vague and evasive manner. At that time I said:
The scope of the conference will he of the fullest breadth. It will be asked to study ways and means of repatriating the constitution; the problem of adequate representation in the public service, in crown corporations and other government agencies; the recommendations of the Therrien report-
Which, as Your Honour knows, was part of the report of the Glassco commission. Continuing, I said:
-the choice of a national flag, and other symbols of our national sovereignty. In brief, the conference will be asked to examine biculturalism and bilingualism in a comprehensive manner.
In the light of events of the last three years, the demand for what was then spoken of has intensified in the intervening years. Sir, tremendous problems are facing us. All kinds of doctrines have been advanced. There was the doctrine of the two nations that was basic to the government three years ago, until the hon. member for Mount Royal decided on a reinterpretation of that concept. There was the theory of opting out, leading to isolation of the province of Quebec. It has now to all intents and purposes gone up in the smoke of the Liberal council fire in Quebec last week.
Then there was the theory of associated states. That was the plaything of the President of the Privy Council for a while who, until the advent of the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, gave the lead to the acceptance of this doctrine.

We took our stand against these things. We were said to be anti-Quebec. The interesting part of it is this. When we stood in this House of Commons against the amending formula, when all the provinces but Quebec had approved of it, it was said by some that ours was an anti-Quebec attitude. Now the premier of Quebec and all his supporters stand where we stood, because we realized that that formula would simply mummify the constitution of Canada.

The government will consult from time to time with civil service associations concerning its policy on bilingualism in order to obtain their point of view-
In other words, we are going to do the thing and then we are going to consult. That is not the attitude which will bring about unity within the nation.
I want to know this, and I think there is reason for my asking the question. What about the 10 per cent merit points which were spoken of so highly very recently and which were announced by the chairman of the Civil Service Commission of Canada? We see nothing about that in the statement. The chairman of the Civil Service Commission said he had a right to bring in these things. I say the Civil Service Act was never intended to be interpreted in this way, and if there are to be any changes in the Civil Service Act those changes should be made in this parliament, not under general sections taken advantage of by the chairman for the purpose.
I want to know whether this 10 per cent additional merit mark is in effect. If it is, I would point out that the civil service employees' organization of the province of Quebec has come out against it as being discrimination against those of French origin. Is this system in effect?

Bilingualism in Public Service
Now, what about some of the other changes? It is most desirable to bring together 20 English families in a French area and 10 French families in an English area, but that is just the icing on the program. It is a fine thing to have the necessary training facilities so that civil servants may become proficient in both languages. But these arrangements are mainly directed toward the future; 1970. After 1970 there will be no promotion unless a candidate is proficient in both languages or expresses a willingness to become so. Recruitment at university level after 1967 will require reasonable proficiency in the two official languages, or willingness to acquire it within a prescribed period of time.
Then the statement goes on to utter these pious words; that the merit system will be fully protected and there will be no prejudice to career civil servants. If the government carries this plan into effect, those words simply are not factually correct. There must be greater assurance that those who are today in the civil service will not, as a result of changes made after their entry into the civil service, be prejudiced in any way.
I shall not go into the other details. Believing as I do in the need of measures to encourage equal partnership-to do what we did, in large measure, to increase the fields of opportunity for those of the French language and race who previously were denied reasonable equality of opportunity-we think this whole matter should be referred to a committee of the House of Commons to secure the fullest possible information and the latest statistics thereon. And then the Civil Service Act should be rewritten by parliament, not by interpretation on the part of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission.
We believe that since this matter is a segment of the larger question of Canadian unity, action such as this should not be taken until the report of the B and B commission is available, and that in any event only such action should be taken as would bring about in this nation a new sense and recognition of the contribution of the two basic races, and of the other races. This was our plan in 1963, which was prevented from implementation only by our defeat at the polls. We had in mind the convening of a national conference on confederation whose purpose and aim would be a declaration of goals for the next 100 years. This provides the only way in which we as Canadians, can satisfactorily look forward to the second century.

The members of the commission staff are not even able to get along or work together to find solutions to the problems, yet they are spending millions of dollars. One wonders how they can spend so much money, unless they are standing on the street corners throwing it away to the public.

It is about time this report was called for. After we have had a chance to study it I think the Prime Minister might be in order in making the same presentation as he made today. I would remind him that there happens to be eight other provinces in this country apart from those two. For all these provinces and their people Ottawa is the capital of our nation too, so I consider that any program should be much broader than the one mentioned by the Prime Minister.

Statement on Wildlife Policy English and French speaking citizens-expressed any interest in the school, and only 43 of these people were within the boundaries of Ottawa.
It seems to me that the Prime Minister, in spite of his sincerity and desire in making 1967, our centennial year, a year of unity, is moving ahead of himself and in so doing is defeating the very objective which is his and to which I believe he is dedicated. I believe that the Prime Minister, in view of what he has said today, has an obligation to this house, to the country and to the government he leads to call for the report of the B and B commission immediately; because, if we are to proceed with the policy he outlined today, there is no justification for that commission continuing its work.
The objective of unity in this country is one that I share and believe in with all my heart, because if we in Canada cannot live together in unity and develop a cohesive nation, what hope is there for the rest of the world? Mr. Speaker, the minister has been kind enough, as has been indicated, to provide copies of the comprehensive statement on wildlife policy. Having had an opportunity to peruse that presentation I should like to make one or two comments.

It is unfortunate that we have not had a government statement on the matter before today because, as all hon. members are aware, that conference took place some five years ago in the city of Montreal. I think it is happy timing, now that this announcement has been made, that it comes on the eve of national wildlife week. It is of course well known that the celebration of this week commences April 10. It is an occasion that is dedicated to the memory of one who is known as the father of conservation, the late Jack Miner. I think it is also significant that it comes in the year in which we shall be

observing the fiftieth anniversary of the signing of the international migratory birds treaty.
I should like to have spoken at greater length on the matter, but I realize that a considerable amount of time has already been taken up in the course of this afternoon's sitting. I would emphasize once again that the time is long past due when we must come to grips with the problem of wise management, on the basis of the multiple use concept, of our renewable resources. This will require implementation of policies at all levels of government.
The statement as I read it is a rehash of many of the ideas, as I have already indicated, that came out of the resources for tomorrow conference. If we are to have government action on these matters the promise that was made almost a year ago to the resource ministers council, when the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources indicated that a wildlife act would be implemented, must be fulfilled at the earliest possible moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING WINTER HOUSE BUILDING INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
On several occasions during the past few weeks, Mr. Speaker, members of this house including my colleague the Minister of Veterans Affairs and officials of Central Mortgage
April 6. 1966

Winter House Building Program and Housing and of the Department of Labour, have discussed with me the matter raised in the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, namely the effect of the flood conditions in Manitoba on the termination date of the winter house building incentive program.
I should like to say, first of all, that some general representations have been received from a few other areas to the effect that the time for completion of houses under the winter house incentive program be extended beyond April 15. These representations have been based on a variety of factors, including climatic conditions and shortages of labour and materials.
Hon. members will recall that during the previous two winters the termination date for construction under this winter house building program was originally set for March 31, but in each case was extended to mid-April. At the commencement of this winter's program the experience of the two previous years was assessed, and it was decided that the terminal date should be established as April 15. In view of this decision, and after reviewing the experience generally throughout Canada this winter, the government is not disposed to consider any further general extension of the period.
The situation in parts of Manitoba, however, is quite different. There is a possible disaster owing to the flood situation in the area between Emerson and Winnipeg. It is not practical, and in many cases not possible, to continue the construction of houses in flooded or potentially flooded areas. In fact I understand Emerson is being evacuated today.
Accordingly the government is giving the winter house building program in the potential disaster area careful study, and special provision will be made with reference to the completion of houses in all areas of Manitoba directly affected by the flood condition. The exact number of houses which may be affected by the flood conditions is not known, but officials of the Department of Labour and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation have been requested to examine each case to determine to what extent a delay in construction has been caused by factors related to the current flood situation in Manitoba. Details as to the special action to be taken will be worked out as circumstances develop.

speechtext:
1.	Have any incidents of disease in the commercial and seed corn crops of southwestern Ontario, particularly in the counties of Essex and Kent, been identified as caused by virus infection?
2.	Have any outbreaks of disease in the commercial and seed corn crops been reported that have been suspected of being, or have been proven to be, caused by the maize dwarf mosaic or any other disease causing the stunting of corn?
3.	Has the government stationed in the immediate area sufficient agricultural technicians (a) to correctly identify any such virus infection (b) to determine whether such disease could be spread by insects and to identify such insects (c) to work out suitable control measures in either of the above instances?
4.	Are any technicians working on this problem directly and, if so, where are they located regarding laboratory facilities, etc.?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. Greene (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: DISEASE IN CORN CROPS, SOUTHWESTERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
1.	Yes. Only wheat streak mosaic virus, which causes mild mottle symptoms in corn, has been identified. Red kernel stripe of corn which was originally suspected of being caused by virus infection has not been confirmed and probably is not virus induced.
2.	No. Maize dwarf mosaic virus is known to occur in the corn areas of the United States but so far no suspected or proven cases have been found in Canada. It is known to be in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys and as far north as southern Ohio. Considerable research is in progress in the U.S.A.
3.	and 4. Adequate attention is given to plant disease problems in the region. One officer at Harrow now works on all corn diseases in southwestern Ontario. He refers any suspected virus diseases to the plant research institute, Ottawa, for expert identification and insect vector relationships. An additional specialist has been engaged, starting in June, to deal specifically with corn virus diseases and will be supported by local entomological staff on the mode of transmission.
Questions

subtopic: FAIR WAGES AND HOURS OF LABOUR ACT
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING HOURS OF WORK, RATES OF PAY, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act. This act was passed originally in 1935, being chapter 39 of the statutes of that year. The purpose of the present bill is to bring the wages and hours standards in this act into conformity with the standards of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code enacted by parliament last year.
It has been the policy of the federal government for many years to establish wages and hours conditions for work on government construction contracts. This act relates to government construction contracts only. The wages required to be paid are the rates found to be prevailing in the district in which the work is to be performed for each class of
April 6, 1966	COMMONS
work. The hours standard, however, was specifically set down on a national rather than a local basis. In the act as it now stands these hours are established at eight hours a day, and 44 hours a week, unless longer hours are authorized in special circumstances.
In accordance with the principles which parliament approved last year in the Canada Labour (Standards) Code, the proposed amendment will make it a condition of a federal government construction contract that $1.25 an hour will be the minimum rate to be paid for work on all such contracts if the prevailing standard for any class of work in any area should be less than $1.25. If it is more, the hourly rate is not changed; we want to be sure that it will be brought up to the minimum rate fixed in the Labour Standards Act. If the bill becomes law the standard work week on federal government construction contracts will be 40 hours rather than the present 44, and an overtime rate of time and one half will be required after 40 hours in a week.
Also in line with the hours of work provisions of the Code, contractors will be permitted to work longer hours than under the existing legislation without the necessity of obtaining a permit. At present a permit is required, if it is found necessary to work more than 44 hours in a week. I might say that a substantial number of permits have been issued when work has had to be completed in a short season or in circumstances where completion of a contract was urgent. It is therefore proposed that the act be amended, in accordance with the bill now before the house, to permit the contractor to work up to 48 hours a week without a permit, so long as the overtime rate is paid after 40 hours.
At the present time a contractor is not penalized in any way if he is found to have failed to carry out the wages and hours conditions of his contract. The government considers that contractors who violate the labour conditions of their contracts should be subject to penalties. Having practised law for many years, it is my opinion that it is absurd to have a situation in which no penalties are provided. Accordingly an amendment is being introduced in the bill which will require that a construction contract shall contain a provision establishing liquidated damages in case of default in carrying out the wages and hours conditions.
In answering the second question asked by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) I would say that over the past year my
DEBATES	3957
Fair Wages and Labour Act predecessor and I, as well as senior officials of my department, have discussed the changes required in the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act with both employer and union representatives of the construction industry. In fact, I had consultation with one of the leaders in the construction industry today. I advised him that following the announcement of government business last night, this bill would be considered in the house today. A number of helpful suggestions were made during the discussions to which I have referred. We have incorporated some of the suggestions in the bill and we shall be discussing others later with industry when the regulations under the act are being revised.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin my remarks in connection with this bill with some general observations regarding government legislation on hours of work and pay per hours of work. In recent years such legislation has become more prevalent in our society. I expect this is because of pressure of certain groups upon the government. We appreciate that legislation in this connection has traditionally served a two fold purpose, namely that of protecting workers against exploitation and contractors against unfair competition. It is very difficult to set a standard of wages and hours of work that would apply equally to all Canadians, because of the different circumstances in rates of pay and relationships between employers and employees in various parts of the country.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
It seems very apparent a serious mistake is being made in this Bill No. C-2, which endeavours to regulate the hours of work performed under government contracts. At times when the work may be taking place many miles from the employee's home, the employee would appreciate the opportunity of spending more time on the job in order to increase his weekly pay. Many of these working conditions can be, and are being, agreed upon between contractors and their employees at the present time. It is my submission that once a contract has been let at a certain figure, the government should no longer dictate to the contractor or his employees. Many construction firms and labour organizations feel very strongly along these lines.
Labour has fought for many years for the right of free negotiation with contractors, and labour representatives do not appreciate undue interference with their negotiations. I
April 6, 1968

Fair Wages and Labour Act could say many things about management and labour relations in other industries and government legislation governing labour. However, since this bill is directed strictly at government contracts, I will confine my remarks to that subject.
I should like to mention further that the kitchen attendants and waiters at two air force bases in my riding received pay increases. However, at the same time their hours of work were reduced to 40 hours a week, so the end result was no increase in take-home pay. This was not what the working people of Canada want in the way of government legislation, and this is especially true at a time when there is a shortage of workers.
There are some changes I should like to see in the bill. The first would be no restriction on the hours of work: all negotiated paid employee contributions should be incorporated into the fair wage, wherever they exist. As we know, there is often a difference in this respect between companies and contractors. Possibly a recognition of the different types of construction work throughout the country is necessary. This suggestion is based on a desire to eliminate difficult and disruptive influences in the industry. I would propose that all conflicts over freely negotiated hours of work should be avoided in all types of construction work in a given labour market.
Then, too, a 30 day limit should be imposed on the registration of any violation of the labour code. If this were done a worker could not come back after one or two years and cause a contractor a great deal of difficulty in attempting to prove there had not been a violation of the labour code. The overtime permit procedure should be limited. I understand that this is being looked after. It has been a nuisance to many contractors when they have been required to get a permit for overtime work, especially on those jobs where the workers desired to work overtime. I would be interested in hearing the minister clarify some of these points.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems utterly ridiculous to me to introduce this bill to amend the fair wages and hours of labour act because, for instance, the minimum wage is set at $1.25 an hour. Here is what paragraph 1 says:
(a) "fair wages" means such wages as are generally accepted as current for competent workmen in the district in which the work is being performed for the character or class of work in which such

workmen are respectively engaged; but shall in all cases be such wages as are fair and reasonable-
And the minimum wage is set at $1.25 an hour for competent workmen.
I understand that the minister will be able to claim that nobody prevents a contractor from paying his employees $1.50 or $2.00 an hour. However, one thing remains; the minimum wage, in view of the cost of living at this time, is clearly insufficient.
Moreover, in the explanatory notes of Bill C-2, one reads:
The main purpose of this bill is to amend the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act to change the general standard of hours of work on federal government contracts from 44 hours in a week to 40 hours-
Let us take the case of a worker who now earns $1.25 an hour. If he works 44 hours a week, his salary is $55 a week. With the new legislation, if his salary remained the same, he would get only $50 a week, that is $5 less than previously.
I do not see in this bill any provision which would guarantee to the worker the same weekly salary, that is the same salary for 40 hours of work that he is now getting for 44 hours of work.
If another worker earns $2 an hour, and works 44 hours a week, he gets $88. If he works only 40 hours a week, he will get only $80, that is a decrease of $8 in his weekly income.
In my opinion, that bill should include some provisions to guarantee that the worker's salary will remain the same for fewer hours of work.
If he only works 40 hours a week, under the new provisions of the act, then his salary should be adjusted accordingly and he should be assured that his take-home pay will not be reduced.
In view of the present economic situation, I think such measures are essential at this time and that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) should state that all workers carrying out federal contracts will actually get the same salary, in spite of shorter working hours, they are now being paid under a 44 hour week.

I might say that this is the third consecutive April that I have had the opportunity in this house to speak on matters pertaining to social security, and I should like to reiterate something I said on two previous occasions in the general area of social security. Over the past 30 years, in our approach to this subject, we have allowed a great many anomalies to creep into the law. In many areas this has been ignored. In my view one of the prime reasons for this is the fact that politicians, being what they are-and this is true at least in part of all parties in this house-have talked from time to time about these measures of social security as a result of pressure being brought to bear on them by various groups in the country. It may well be that the course of action advocated is justified. Of
April 6, 1966

course it may be that the justification has been helped greatly by the pressures placed on various politicians to do these things.
In common with other hon. members, I feel that in many instances, and perhaps in the vast majority of cases, $75 a month is not at all sufficient for the old people of this country.
Reference was made, Mr. Speaker, by the hon. member who preceded me in this debate, to the way he conducted his campaign. Judging by the results and by the many elections he has fought, he undoubtedly conducted himself very well because he is now a most successful member of this house. I congratulate him for that. He made reference to the question of this $100 a month. I, too, would like to make reference to the type of campaign conducted in St. John's West, Newfoundland, and to that conducted by my colleague from St. John's East (Mr. O'Keefe). Both of us conducted our campaign in a manner consistent with what we both have said in this house. Really, all that we have done in social security is to approach it from a broad and comprehensive approach. Many areas of need exist.
I know if the hon. gentleman who spoke were to refer to his mail from his constituents, he would find what I have found. I realize from the many letters I have received, that many people who are not old age pensioners, are looking for assistance. As a result of this, over the past few years I have had an opportunity of making a relatively complete study of the type of assistance that is available to various groups, including old age pensioners, in this country. I refer to those groups who are very much in need of assistance.
Anyone who looks at the facts will find out that while $75 a month may never be adequate, there are many other groups of people in this country who have to survive on much less. I refer particularly to widows with young families. There are many other people falling into this class. I know of many persons in my constituency belonging to that group who might be termed the forgotten people of Canada.
Therefore, any government which is to deal with the problem of social security, if it is really to hold true to the principles of social justice must look at the whole area of need to determine what can be done on the basis of the resources available to the country.
When one makes a statement like that I suppose it is like Abraham Lincoln's definition of the responsibilities of government.
Old Age Security Act Anybody can agree with it. A person of a conservative viewpoint can say, "That is very practical" and a person with a radical viewpoint may say the same thing. What really determines the difference is the way we apply this principle of social justice, personally.
Over the years we may have had periods in our history when we have not paid enough attention to social security. However, in the last few years perhaps we have been paying more attention to social security than we had before that time. The result is that today there is a greater awareness than ever before. There is a greater awareness now than there was even a couple of years ago on the part of members of the House of Commons and on the part of the public generally about social security. Not only old age pensioners but a great many other groups of people need to be attended to by the federal government. Many areas of social security are within the jurisdiction of the provinces. We find that one of the difficulties is in the field of the financial abilities of various provinces to cope with this situation.
Therefore, in answer to the hon. member's speech, I hope that when the resolution on the order paper to which he made reference comes before this house for debate he will give it his full support. I say that, because I think that this Canada Assistance Plan is an enlightened and certainly a much needed approach to social security. It will cover for the first time not only old age pensioners, who are very much the concern of this resolution, but other groups as well.
There are various ways in which the $100 a month can be financed. I think it is to these that the most practical considerations of any government must go. For instance, if we were to grant across the board $100 a month to old age pensioners, we know that it would cost in the vicinity of $800 million. Were the government to incur that kind of expenditure, what would happen to other programs for other people in need?
Many other social demands besides the one raised in the resolution are placed on the government. Those demands include such fields as education, retraining of the unemployed and other very necessary social programs which could have an impact on the economy of our country. When we talk about $100 a month, we must determine what it is that we are really trying to do. We must relate this to the cost, and we must try to come up with the best way of doing it.

April 6, 1966
Old Age Security Act
In the light of the present circumstances I know that it is much easier for any politician to go out on the hustings and say to the constituents, "Well, we are going to give $100 straight across the board" because that covers those who need the money very much; it covers those who have less need for the money, and it covers those who perhaps do not have a need for it. The point is that it will cost the treasury a considerable amount of money.
It may be that any government happening to be in office, be it Liberal, Conservative, or otherwise, were it to raise the old age pension would tend to think it had done something wonderful in social security, and therefore would continue to neglect some other areas of need.
May I say that I think there are other ways at this time by which we can accomplish the purposes implicit in the resolution now before the house. That is to say, we may be able to provide additional assistance to old age pensioners through the Canada Assistance Plan which will be coming before the house at an early date. I am afraid I cannot comment on it. However, I am sure that it will meet with the approval of members of the house. In saying that I know that there will be hon. members who will feel that they would rather see an increase to a straight $100, because they will be afraid that under the Canada Assistance Plan there may be certain areas of need, as in the case of old age pensioners, which will not be met because ten provinces of Canada will be doing the administering, and perhaps for other reasons. I feel that by the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan the government is, in part, meeting the problem implicit in the resolution before the house today.
There may be other ways to approach this matter. Many hon. members in the house were particularly attracted to the Senate report, commonly referred to as the Croll report. It appeals to me, because in the administrative sense it seems in terms of social justice to guarantee practically a minimum income to our older Canadians.
I think that is the direction in which this country ought to be heading. In matters of social security in the past, that has been our approach. It has been the peculiar position of the federal government as related to other fields of need, which has caused it to branch into those other areas of social need. Therefore I say again that while our approach to the problem of old age pensions may not be

all that perhaps it ought to be, it is more comprehensive than is the approach to almost any other area of social security.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
So, if we move in the direction of providing a minimum income for older people I think we shall be accepting this principle of guaranteed minimum incomes and that we would go on from there at some later date in our development to making guaranteed minimum incomes available to other categories of people. This is, if you will, the cleanest way, the most honest way and the fairest way in which to meet this pressing social problem.
In the 30 years or more which have passed in this country since we began dealing with social security in a serious way we have built up a program based on a philosophy which is today, in my view, outdated. It has been based on the philosophy of the hand-out. I think this kind of approach is being taken far less frequently by members of all parties in this house, although I am dismayed from time to time when I attend meetings of boards of trade and similar bodies and find people there, no doubt with good intentions, still behaving as if welfare represented a kind of drain from the people who have to the people who have not, whereas what we are trying to do in reality is to give various classes of people better opportunities to fulfil themselves as Canadians.
We should remember that there are many groups of people, scattered and hidden throughout this country, who do not now receive even the level of assistance which is available to our old age pensioners. Many of them are not yet 50. They include widows with families, young people who have dropped out of school and who cannot find suitable jobs, people who have to draw social assistance-all of them people whose dignity is being severely damaged. I recognize the honest differences we may have on this subject, but the fact that so much was said during the past election campaign about this $100, important as it may be, could lead to our forgetting some of these other claims. When we talk about old age pensioners and their pressing needs we should remember there are many other groups in this country for whom little has been done up to now, either by Liberal or by Conservative governments to bring them into line with the benefits now available to our senior citizens.
This is, in part, a constitutional problem-at least, a constitutional problem presents itself in one piece of legislation to which
April 6, 1966



the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) had made reference. I hope that when these matters are discussed further during the course of the next few months we shall all examine them in an effort to find the best and most acceptable way, both in terms of economics and of social justice, of providing pensioners with the assistance they need, and in this way help to establish a more comprehensive approach toward social security in this country than in the past.

Like the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) I shall keep my remarks very brief because I should like to see this motion voted on by the house. I congratulate the hon. member for Grey-Bruce not only on presenting this motion but on the luck of the draw which enabled his motion to be discussed before some others. There are three or four motions on the order paper under the heading of private members' business including one in my name, all of which seek the same end, namely an increase in the old age pension to $100 a month and the lowering of the age of eligibility to 65 years right away.
I support this proposition. I have supported it for so long that I hardly need say so. I also wish to make the point that if we are to reform parliament and get some business done here it might be a good thing once in a while to let a private member's motion such as this come to a vote. All the motion says is that in the opinion of the house the government should consider providing $100 a month at age 65.
When this question was before us in two amendments during the debate on the address there were procedural arguments and it was suggested that the passing of either of those amendments would cause the defeat of the government. The passing of this motion would not cause the defeat of the government. It would simply express an opinion of the house, and I believe if the house were free to express its opinion on this issue, as it has been on other issues, it would be categorically in favour of the motion before us.
Old Age Security Act
I listened with interest to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin). He took 15 minutes to tell us what he wanted to say. But what did he say? Really, all he said was that there are other areas where something needs to be done just as urgently as something needs to be done for the old age pensioners. But he did not say when or where we should move. As a matter of fact I believe his speech added up to the using of these other areas as an excuse for doing nothing to raise the old age pension, and I suggest that is not good enough.

Yes, I know the hon. member referred to the Canada Assistance Plan. We have been trying to get the government to proceed with that for a full year. But again he is using that plan, as well as other things undefined, as an excuse for opposing the motion put down by the hon. member for Grey-Bruce.
I do not take second place to the hon. member for St. John's West in my belief that the Canada Pension Plan is good legislation. Indeed, I believe we have got many pieces of worthwhile social legislation on the statute books of this country, put there by the governments which have held office over the years, even if under pressure from some of us. But I think our package of social legislation will not be good enough for Canada in the sixties as long as we leave the old age pension at its present figure of $75. Even though people will begin getting the benefit of the Canada Pension Plan in some future year, I believe, as one who has studied this matter carefully, that at the present moment the level of our old age pension should be brought up to $100 a month.
I am asking the house today to let us have a vote on this issue to see whether this is not the opinion of the members of the House of Commons. The government can then decide whether it wishes to pay some attention to that opinion. Surely we have the right once in a while in private members' hour to express our opinion by a vote. The hon. member for St. John's West made a remark about the mail we get from our constituents. This is something which, I think, impresses all of us. Anyone who has been around here as long as I have gets a great deal of mail, and during

April 6, 1966
Old Age Security Act the present session there have been many subjects on which people have been writing us. But in my experience it is still the hundreds of letters from older people telling me of their plight, of their difficulty in trying to get along on $75 a month, which outdistance all the mail I get on all the other subjects. If this is my experience I suggest it is probably the experience of a good many other members of this house.
It is also a fact that all the responsible social agencies in the country have established that an older person simply cannot get along on less than $110, $115 or $130 a month-different organizations have arrived at different figures.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
I submit that with these facts staring us in the face, as presented to us by social work organizations, concerning the conditions which our older people face, and as presented to us in the letters our pensioners write to us, that we in this House of Commons ought to have the heart, the decency and the responsibility to act on this motion.
I would like to speak on it at length, Mr. Speaker, but I am pleading for a vote, and therefore I conclude these remarks at this point and urge the house to support this motion for raising old age security to $100 a month right away.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) for having introduced this resolution, and having put it on the order paper, to ask that the old age pension be raised to $100 a month and the age of eligibility of applicants be set at 65 years instead of 70 years as it is today.
While the mover was explaining why his motion should be adopted, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) intervened to ask if he thought we should raise taxes or include such an increase in the Canada pension plan. The Minister of Finance seemed to wonder where he could find the money to pay $100 to persons of 65 and over. I think that we are taking this matter a little too lightly in this house.
We do think of our old people, but not seriously enough. Like any other member of the cabinet, the Minister of Finance knows very well that a pension of $75 is inadequate at the present time and, during the last

election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), the head of government, promised up to $125 a month to those of our senior citizens who were in need.
But now, four and a half months after the election, the Minister of Finance is worrying about where to find the money to raise old age pensions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCREASE PENSIONS
speechtext: May I say to the hon. member, Mr. Speaker, that I did not ask that question. I asked the hon. member who was speaking at the time whether he intended to finance this out of the Canada Pension Plan, as had been advocated by his party. It is quite obvious where the money would come from: It would come from the taxpayers.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO INCREASE PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. Minister of Finance for making known his stand, but I do not agree with him in that the money required to increase old age pensions would have to be taken out of the pockets of Canadian taxpayers. We now have several plans in Canada: the Canada pension plan, old age security, unemployment insurance, unemployment assistance, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Act, and coming medicare, all kinds of plans, the cost of which will be met through taxes.
Now, there is another way of financing an increase in old age pension, of financing social security in Canada. And that method, the Minister of Finance knows what it is. It is the full use of the Bank of Canada in making financially possible what is physically achievable. Instead of calling it a plan, a "master plan", let us call it a national dividend from the new credits of the Bank of Canada.
It is strange, but when war comes, the Minister of Finance does not wonder where the money will come from. The minister knows that in 1939, when war broke out, the government of the day did not go to the taxpayers for money, because they had not had a cent for some ten years, since the beginning of the depression. We went to the Bank of Canada. The Minister of Finance at that time, Mr. Ilsley, managed to use the Bank of Canada credits, to summon forth, right across the country, such war industries as no country in the world has ever known.
It was possible then to find the money and to set up a tremendous war machine in Canada. When it comes to social security, the Minister of Finance will ask us: where will the money be found, where will it come
April 6, 1966

from? From the pockets of Canadian taxpayers? Let us be logical, and let us face the facts.
The Minister of Finance is aware that the Canadian people are making superhuman efforts and are ready to keep on contributing to the economic development of our country, to the establishment of new industries and to the increase of Canadian productivity. The Minister of Finance is aware of this. But in his budget, he checks the economic development of the country and he will create more unemployment and slow down the progress of the Canadian economy.
The increase in old age pensions must not result in a decrease of the purchasing power of other elements or social classes of our society. Is Canada able to produce enough goods to guarantee to all those who are 65 or over an income of $100 a month? Is Canada capable of producing enough clothing, food, housing, for all our elderly people to live decently in our country? Has Canada the physical possibilities to make life happier for our old people? The Minister of Finance does not ask himself those questions because he knows that Canada can do it, that the production is there, that our stores, our industries are full of all kinds of goods. We are not lacking in clothing, wood, manpower, goodwill, to develop the country.
And the main question which keeps coming up in the house as well as outside is the financial question: Where will the money come from? The taxpayers will pay, the Canadian taxpayers will be taxed more.
Mr. Speaker, when we tax the worker and the farmer, when the government taxes the people, we diminish the purchasing power of that class by that much.
Why not resort to the redistribution of wealth in Canada? If some requisites are taken away from someone earning $5,000 a year to be given to one who earns nothing, the over-all purchasing power of the Canadian people is not increased in any way.
We, in the Ralliement Creditiste, suggest the implementation of the social credit principle to pay a national dividend, not out of thin air but based on what the Canadian people create through productivity.
This year, in 1966-1967, we are advised by the government-and the Minister of Finance said so in his Budget speech-that Canada will produce approximately $54 to $55 billion worth of consumer goods or services. Faced with this huge production, the 23033-251
Old Age Security Act Canadian people as a whole, and not only in part, will have a total national income of about $40 to $42 billion. There will be a difference of $12 to $13 billion because the government does not try to balance production and the purchasing power or the taxpayers' income.
Mr. Speaker, the Social credit doctrine has been expounded in this house by members from Alberta for nearly 25 or 30 years. Since 1935, members outlined here the Creditists' theory or the Social credit doctrine, but the government has always turned a deaf ear. Instead of gearing the financial system to the production system, the government tries to adjust the production system to the financial system.
Instead of making financially possible what is physically possible, the government tries to make physically possible what is financially possible. Production is adjusted to finance, instead of finance being adjusted to production. That is the weakness of the present system.
Does the minister want to put a question?

Instead of fitting finance to material possibilities, efforts are made to adjust material possibilities to financial possibilities.

As the need for war plants, guns, clothing and feeding soldiers arose, the government found the necessary credits. The minister knows that. But with peace, and for the preservation of peace, the minister can no longer find the money to guarantee economic security and personal liberty to each and every Canadian citizen.

April 6, 1966

In wartime, there were jobs for all Canadian young men and women and there were no unemployed in Canada. But, the minister says it is financially impossible to do it in time of peace. We will not accept this constant tight credit policy, Mr. Speaker.

However, I wanted to insist that funds must be found to increase old age pensions to $100 per month.
Now, the present government does not have the means to finance these pension increases. All the government does, is to make promises at election time and to forget those same promises the day after the election. That is all it does.
I suggested the Bank of Canada to the government as a means to finance old age pension increase.
We have been demanding $100 per month for our senior citizens in Canada for the last ten years; with the rise in the cost of living, we will some day ask for $125 per month at age 60, because people 60 years of age can no longer find employment to make a living; even at 40, they are considered too old.
Mr. Speaker, these are considerations that we must eventually face. I do not want to prevent the vote from being taken on this resolution, but I want to give the Liberals an opportunity to prove they are sincere. If they are so desirous of helping the elderly in Canada, they will let the vote be taken on the motion this afternoon.

The Ralliement creditiste will vote in favour of an increase of the old age pension to $100 at 65 years of age-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on an occasion such as this I think the sincerity of one's support for a motion of this kind is indicated more clearly by allowing it to come to a vote than by indulging in a multitude of words. However, I do want to state categorically that we in the Social Credit party are in full support of the resolution now before us, and we intend to give it our support if the government will allow it to come to a vote before six o'clock.
I do not think there is any question in anyone's mind regarding the necessity for an increase in old age security to $100 per month. On a number of occasions we have received communications from individuals who are endeavouring to get by on the present pension of $75 per month. They have provided us with lists of groceries, and their other costs, to show the increase in the cost of living that has taken place over a short period of time.
Here in this house it has been brought to our attention that there has been a constant increase in the cost of living, and we have been warned that this increase will continue throughout this year. For that reason I do not think anyone can argue that an increase in old age pensions is out of line. We hope therefore, that other members will have an opportunity this afternoon to support this resolution and vote on it.
A short time ago we in this party had the opportunity of presenting a compromise formula to the government for its consideration. We did so because the government had indicated quite clearly that it was not prepared to grant $100 per month old age pension at age 65. We regret there has not been any response whatsoever to this compromise proposal, and we must come to the conclusion that the government has not been sincere in its quest for a formula whereby old age
April 6, 1966

pensions could be increased to bring some relief, especially to those who are in dire need.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Cashin) referred to the fact that our proposal would cost in the neighbourhood of $800 million. We do not accept that suggestion because old age pensions are universal and there would be a return in the form of income taxes. Of course other types of assistance would be eliminated, and this would drastically reduce the cost from $800 million.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Therefore we believe the government should move in line with the recommendations of this motion. We also call the attention of the government to the fact that veterans, superannuated civil servants and other categories of senior citizens are still awaiting some definite consideration. Many of these people are living in conditions almost of destitution. I have received from a number of old age pensioners organizations the request that we have a free vote on this particular measure. We were allowed a free vote on the matter that was decided yesterday. I realize there is of course a difference in the issue that was before us then and that which is before us now, but it is very difficult for senior citizens to understand why a free vote can be allowed on one issue but not on another that so vitally affects their interests. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the suggestion is made that this matter should come to a vote today as an indication of the feeling of the house for the guidance and direction of the government in its consideration of this issue.
I would suggest that a vote be taken this evening in order to obtain the decision of the house. I would further suggest that the government should take the result of the vote into very serious consideration. In the debate that was concluded last evening-I shall not refer to it in detail-it was said that treatment of the misfits in our society is a measure of the stature of our nation. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I suggest that the treatment of our senior citizens is a measure of the stature of our nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it amused me somewhat to hear several members clamour for the vote, and then, all of them took the time to speak just the same. One spoke for 29 minutes, another for 14 minutes, and so on. This
Old Age Security Act being so, Mr. Speaker, everybody here would claim his right to speak in this house. I know members on both sides who would like to speak about old age security.
Everybody agrees, I think, that the situation of our old people should be improved. It is a matter of considering the best procedure to be followed for that purpose.
In my opinion, it is not realistic to give $100 to persons of 65, because some of them really need $150 at that age, while others would still not be getting enough, and for others still, $150 would be luxury.
Therefore, I feel that the whole social security program should be reviewed.
A member of the Ralliement Creditiste mentioned an aspect that should be taken into consideration. As things are, obtaining a pension at 65 leads some people to think they are getting old in our society, whereas between 60 and 65, jobs are getting scarce. This is not realistic.
I believe the whole social assistance system should at all costs be revised and reviewed, in a practical way, according to the needs of 1966. Consideration should therefore be given to the manpower program, for instance, as well as to the retraining of the unskilled worker, in short, jobs should be found for those between 55 and 60 years when they are no longer able to work.
The needs of old people should also be taken into consideration, because, as I said earlier, for a few of them, $150 a month would not be enough.
Even if partisanship is forbidden, even if it is said that no political capital should be made out of this question, I believe that efforts are being made to embarrass the government and I shall believe it until I am shown it is not so.
It was stated a while ago, across the floor, that the government did not seem sincere. It nevertheless remains that a bill on social security was announced and it seems to be rather comprehensive. It has not been submitted to us, but if it contains provisions to ensure a guaranteed income to our old people, according to their needs, and if it provides for additional benefits, for instance, when their health makes it impossible for them to survive with the present allowance, in short, if special allowances are paid without too many restrictions and red tape, I think their needs will be more adequately met than if we were to grant them a $100 pension at age 65. It was the leader of the

April 6, 1966
Old Age Security Act Ralliement creditiste (Mr. Caouette) who suggested at one time that the pension be set according to the cost of living. That would be more realistic, for it is possible that a $100 pension at age 65 may not be realistic at some future time.
I think a vote at this time would settle nothing. First, the house is now in a minority. It would only embarrass those people who are unanimous in wishing the old people well.
In these circumstances, I think all opposition parties are helping the government by leaving it no peace, by reminding it of its responsibility to do something to meet the needs, not only the old people aged 65, 66 or 70 but of all those in our midst who need to live properly according to 1966 standards. The unemployed, for instance, those who, because of social conditions, cannot find employment, must also be our concern as much as the old people.
Consequently, I suggest to the opposition to keep on harassing the government for a comprehensive social legislation to solve the whole problem, covering all those in need, in a society as affluent as ours where it is inconceivable, even today, to find poverty when so many things go to waste.
I am not concerned about the financial aspect of the matter, for I know that when a practical plan to meet such needs is found, what is materially necessary will be made financially possible.

Introduction
Wildlife, a renewable resource, is one of Canada's great heritages. Yet not enough is being done to ensure its future usefulness to Canadians. As the economy expands, as Canadians find more leisure time at their disposal, as urban development impinges on wildlife habitat, and as farmers and foresters adopt new techniques to protect and improve their crops, the pressures on wildlife steadily mount.
Wildlife contributes to the national economy and provides millions of man-hours of priceless outdoor recreation. There are over 1,000,000 hunters in Canada. In recent years they have spent about $100 million annually in pursuing their sport.
A great number of Canadians and foreign visitors use the resource in other ways: they look at wildlife, travelling many miles to do so, and study and photograph wildlife. Wildlife is a major attraction for visitors to both National and Provincial parks. There were over nine million visitors to our National Parks in 1965.
The demand for wildlife for both hunting and non-consumptive uses seems to increase with population growth and the rising standard of living. Evidence from the United States and Great Britain indicates that the increase in demand continues as the human population grows. So the need to preserve wildlife will become even more urgent.
The supply of wildlife has generally grown smaller as the number of Canadians and visitors to Canada has grown larger. Drainage of wetlands, destruction of natural cover for the building of cities, the improvement and extension of farms, the growing of trees, and the flooding of lands behind large dams have all reduced the area of habitat for many species. Wildlife numbers depend upon the extent and quality of available habitat, just as the numbers of livestock depend upon the quality and quantity of range.
Jurisdiction over wildlife is divided between Canada and the provinces. Canada has a responsibility for migratory birds, for wildlife in the National Parks, and for those species in the Northwest Territories declared by the Governor in Council to be in danger of extinction. The provinces and the Territories have full responsibility for all other wildlife, but the benefits of wildlife can accrue to all Canadians and some national perspective toward the resource is long overdue.
Means by which national concern about wildlife can best be translated into effective action have been discussed by representatives of Canada and the provinces at meetings of the Canadian Council of Resource Ministers, the Federal-Provincial Wildlife Conference, and the Prime Minister's and Premiers' Conference in July 1965. It has been agreed that the Federal Government should take positive action for the conservation of migratory birds and their habitat, and that federal assistance should be made available in respect of wildlife coming under provincial jurisdiction.
The policy and program outlined herein have been developed to meet the needs expressed by conservationists and wildlife officials throughout Canada by means in accordance with principles generally endorsed by responsible Ministers.
In brief, the program to be developed under our general wildlife policy includes supporting and undertaking fundamental research in support of wildlife management throughout Canada, provision of information about wildlife, and co-operation with the provinces, on request and by agreement, in attaining the goals of wildlife management. The program also includes an increase in activities related to the federal responsibilities for migratory birds, wildlife in National

General Wildlife Policy
1.	The Federal Government will undertake research on the relationship between wildlife and forests. This program will be integrated with basic studies of forest ecology and productivity being carried on by the Department of Forestry. Objectives will be to determine factors affecting wildlife populations supported by various types of forests, the effects of varying populations of wildlife on the forests, and the effects of forestry practices on wildlife populations.
2.	The Federal Government will undertake research on factors affecting the health of wildlife populations. Diseases, parasitic infections, pesticides and other environmental pollutants have important effects on wildlife populations in all parts of Canada. Studies of those factors are specialized occupations calling for a high degree of training and adequate laboratory support and it is unlikely that those requirements will be met in all provinces. The Federal Government must develop facilities for such studies to meet its own responsibilities. Pesticides and many diseases affect more than one member of an animal community, so the information obtained will be useful to all governments.
The following programs are planned:
(a)	Systematic assessment of the occurrence and significance of diseases and parasites affecting Canadian wildlife populations (some of which indirectly affect humans as well).
(b)	Determination of the effects of pesticide-use programs on wildlife populations.
(c)	Maintenance of a central registry of information on pesticide characteristics, pesticide residues in wildlife, and diseases and parasites if they relate to wildlife. Information will be provided to other governments on request.
(d)	Development and maintenance of a national reference collection of wildlife parasites and disease organisms.
3.	Wildlife research services may be provided to provinces on request and by agreement if it is apparent that the Federal Government is best equipped to deal with the problems concerned.
4.	The Federal Government may support research and management related to wide-ranging wildlife populations. Some wildlife
populations, for example, barren-ground caribou, move across provincial boundaries and thus come under the jurisdiction of more than one government. Co-ordinated or cooperative research and management are usually necessary if such populations are to thrive. Agreements may be concluded with provinces desiring to participate in co-operative research or management of populations that are not confined to one province.
5.	The Federal Government's information program will be designed to serve the interests of all governments wherever possible. The dissemination of information about wildlife by all media is a powerful means of improving the quality of wildlife management and securing public acceptance of management measures. The principles of wildlife management are the same whatever species or groups of species may be involved, although the details of application may vary. Bulletins, brochures, and films prepared primarily to convey information about wildlife subject to federal responsibility may thus usefully and easily be modified to serve a broader purpose.
6.	The Federal Government will act to improve the supply of professionally trained wildlife biologists. Prospective entrants to the field should be encouraged, and research carried on in the universities as an aspect of their graduate training program should be supported.
Two activities are under way and will be expanded:
(a)	Needed researches in the wildlife field that can be effectively undertaken by university staff members and graduate students are being supported by contracts.
(b)	Scholarships are being offered to graduate students in wildlife and allied fields.
Migratory Birds
General Policy
1.	Every effort will be made to prevent the extinction of any species. Special protection of the birds and their habitat, and artificial propagation may be employed.
2.	Bird populations should be managed so that they are maintained at levels as nearly as possible in harmony with man's various interests. Such a concept of optimum population size is useful, even though optima cannot yet be defined for more than a few species. Limitations of habitat and conflict between birds and man's other interests set the upper
