limit of optimum populations. Human demand and the danger of extirpation set the lower limit. Populations of most ducks should be maintained as nearly as possible within the high and low levels that existed during the period 1950-56. Such populations will ensure survival of all species, provide some opportunity for hunting and other recreational pursuits in Canada and the United States for the foreseeable future, yet not give rise to insoluble problems of crop damage. Populations of most geese could usefully be maintained at somewhat higher levels than have existed in recent years. As opportunity permits, or circumstances require, studies should be directed toward defining optimum populations of other migratory birds. If actual populations are not in line with defined optima, means should be devised to bring them to the desired level.
3.	All Canadians should have an opportunity to share in the use of the resource, and those who use it should contribute by user fee to the costs of management.
4.	Because migratory birds move back and forth across the continent, intergovernmental and international consultation, co-ordination, and co-operation in research and management will be continued and expanded.
Maintenance and Management of Migratory Bird Habitat
1.	Survival of migratory birds is dependant upon maintenance of habitat. Suitable wetland habitat in amounts sufficient to support desired populations of ducks and geese will be preserved by acquisition, lease, or other form of agreement.
2.	Agreements may be concluded with provinces desiring to participate in acquisition or management of habitat, the terms of agreement to be compatible with the national objective of maintaining desired populations and distribution of migratory birds and to provide security for the federal investment.
3.	Some of the areas acquired in fee simple or to which agreements pertain may require no management other than that required to maintain them in their natural state. For many others, the pressure for an increased supply of birds and the need to get the highest return for the public investment will call for development and improvement. Thus, when it is economically feasible, habitat will be improved so as to increase its carrying capacity for and productivity of birds. This may be done by controlling water levels, altering natural plant cover, and creating
nesting and resting sites. It is desirable that this be done so far as possible without adversely affecting the aesthetic quality of the landscape.
4.	Habitat may be managed so as to influence the local distribution of birds and thus reduce the possibility and extent of damage to agricultural crops and other interests. Management plans for all areas where significant damage by birds occurs or may occur will include features designed to eliminate or minimize damage. Provision of food to attract birds away from commercial crops is the principal technique presently employed.
5.	Land managed for migratory birds should be available for public use so far as possible. In most cases, the public should have access to habitat under public control in order to watch, study, or photograph the birds. In many cases, such lands may support concentrations of birds of sufficient size that hunting is desirable. In any case, management will involve controlling public activity so that it does not damage the habitat or undesirably disturb the birds. Public use may be subject to a user fee. Arrangements in this regard may be a part of agreements with provinces.
6.	Land secured primarily for preservation of migratory bird habitat may be used for other productive purposes, if they are not incompatible. Where such is the case, and there is local need and economic justification for it, such uses may be permitted by agreement with provinces, other government agencies, corporations, or individuals.
7.	Two programs to acquire adequate control of wetland habitat are planned:
(a)	Conclusion of agreements with landowners whereby they agree not to drain or fill the wetlands which they own, or burn the vegetation around them, in return for a payment based on the value of the surrounding land discounted at five per cent for a 20-year period. Using this procedure to maintain about two-thirds of the more than six million small potholes in the vitally important prairie breeding grounds should provide habitat for populations within the 1950-56 levels.
(b)	Purchase or long term lease of large marshes which require management for great productivity and public use. Large marshes are important not only as breeding areas but also as areas where the birds may winter or rest during migration. They are also the areas where much of the hunting takes place. Some

The magnitude of a program to preserve all such areas, and the priorities for acquisition, cannot be finally determined until the ARDA-sponsored Land Capability Inventory, now under way, is completed and studied.
Control of Migratory Bird Harvest
1.	A sustained yield of migratory game birds should be secured at as high a level as availability of habitat and risk of damage to other interests will permit. Within the limits imposed by the natural distribution of populations, all Canadians should have equal opportunity for a fair share of the harvest.
2.	Given adequate habitat, regulation of the harvest is the principal means of population control. Regulation of the opening dates, season lengths, bag limits, and zones governing hunting will have the primary objective of maintaining overwintering populations at a level in harmony with the ability of the habitat to support them. Risk of unforeseen natural hazards, the existence of a presently unknown margin of error in population data, and the unpredictability of weather conditions that affect hunting seasons demand a conservative approach to the establishment of regulations.
3.	Other objectives of regulations will be to reduce the waste of birds by crippling, to reduce the risk of accidents, and, so far as possible, to provide equivalent hunting opportunity to all Canadians. In addition, regulations will be drafted with a view to the practicality of their enforcement.
4.	Equitable opportunity to harvest depends upon observance of the regulations governing hunting. Illegal over-harvest is equivalent to the theft of public property. Enforcement and information programs designed to secure conformity of hunting practices with regulations will be expanded and improved.
5.	Special temporary provision will be made for privileged use of migratory birds by persons who, because of their place or mode of living, require the resource for subsistence. The legal basis for such provisions, which are especially necessary to some Eskimos and Indians, is not clear, nor will their administration be easy. Solution of both the legal and administrative problems will be given high priority.
Migratory Bird Research
The primary objective of research is to secure information that will enable effective management. In the process the sum of human knowledge of our natural environment is increased.
Research Related to Habitat
1.	Since migratory bird management involves management of habitat as well, some research must be directed toward obtaining information on habitat characteristics and the complex interrelationships among living things that share the same space.
2.	A major objective of migratory bird habitat research is to develop better methods of evaluating the habitat required for all stages in the life cycles of the various species. Contributing to this end are studies of rates of occurrence of birds in different areas and comparisons of growth, survival, behaviour, and use made of food and cover plants in each type of area. Data obtained will be basic to an improved classification of migratory bird habitat, as well as a more effective method of evaluation.
3.	Research is required to provide the information necessary to develop methods of improving the usefulness of habitat at lowest cost. Studies of the characteristics and usefulness of natural habitat are basic, and yield the information to plan experimental modification of water levels, plant cover, etc.
4.	Development of effective and economic methods of alleviating damage by birds to other interests requires investigation of the characteristics, extent, and severity of damage.
5.	If land is to be used for more than one purpose, the requirements of the several purposes must be clearly understood. Thus, to develop plans for multiple use of wildlife habitat, the results of wildlife research must be considered in conjunction with information obtained during studies of other land uses, such as grazing, forestry, etc.
Research Related to Populations
1.	Research on migratory birds themselves has the objective of maintaining current, accurate information on their population levels and distribution, and developing an understanding of the operation of factors affecting the numbers and distribution of the birds.
2.	The demand-supply squeeze on ducks and geese necessitates development and perfection

of systems for accurate and continuing measurements of their populations. Present systems include aerial and ground censuses of populations on the breeding grounds in spring, midsummer surveys to provide data for an estimate of productivity, and posthunting season surveys on the wintering grounds. Most of the relevant work in Canada is carried on by the United States. Canadian participation will be extended with the eventual objective of assuming major responsibility within Canada.
3.	The use of waterfowl by hunters should be measured so that there can be an annual balancing of population gains and losses. This can be done most effectively by a National Kill Survey that will be carried out by mail questionnaires directed to a sample of persons hunting waterfowl. The statistical universe from which the sample will be selected will be provided by a list of the names and addresses of hunters purchasing the Canada Migratory Game Bird Hunting Permit. All hunters of migratory birds will be required to hold a Canada Migratory Game Bird Hunting Permit, although it will be issued free of charge to Indians and Eskimos. This survey and associated enquiries will also yield information on the species of birds hunted, as well as when and where they are hunted. That sort of information will permit an evaluation of the effects of changes in regulation that has not previously been possible.
4.	Factors other than hunting affect migratory bird populations and, if changes in population levels are to be understood and at least partially controlled, research on those other factors is required. Studies based on recoveries of banded birds yield information on survival rates, distribution, and movements. Field studies of breeding success and other phases of life history contribute to understanding of factors affecting populations. Effects of diseases, parasitic infections, and the use of pesticides can be significant and require continued study.
National Parks Wildlife General Policy
1.	Wildlife in National Parks is an important part of the national heritage and should be preserved unimpaired for the benefit, education, and enjoyment of future generations. It is, therefore, part of the national park purpose to maintain healthy populations of native animals, including predators, in balance with their environment.
2.	Wildlife is an element of the natural ecological communities in National Parks. Such communities, including the wildlife components, may require management to maintain healthy forest and other vegetative cover, to control erosion, and to preserve recreational and aesthetic values. Management should be kept to a minimum in order to maintain aesthetic values of, at least, a quasi-natural environment.
3.	National Park planning should give full consideration to character, size, shape, and location of park areas in order to provide for the year-round ecological requirements of the indigenous animal species, especially those with migratory habits.
4.	Conflicts between wildlife and other park interests including human safety should be resolved if possible without destruction of wildlife. When removal or destruction of animals is decided upon on the basis of research findings, it should be done by Departmental employees and as promptly and unobtrusively as possible.
5.	Adequate stocks of fish should be provided and maintained through modern methods of management where they can be applied without detriment to the aesthetic values of the areas concerned.
Parks Wildlife Research
1.	Wildlife research is an integral part of National Park purposes where data are required to establish appropriate public activities and sound management of the natural features. Wildlife research for other than park purposes may be carried on in parks, if such study is otherwise in harmony with parks policy and if no areas suitable for its conduct can be found elsewhere.
2.	Wildlife research in parks will be oriented toward studies of animals in their total environment, since the objective is to maintain environments that reflect a minimum human impact. Studies of range and habitat conditions and of the factors affecting population levels are basic. Priority will be given to studies helpful in devising means of maintaining habitat capable of supporting desired populations.
3.	Studies of health and condition factors are of particular importance in parks, where populations are often limited by the extent of available habitat.
4.	Studies basic to the develpment of suitable methods of controlling size and distribution of animals to maintain them in balance

with their environment and to prevent conflict with other interests are of particular importance in parks.
5.	Research oriented toward the maintenance of adequate stocks of fish is essential. Subjects of research should include productivity of park waters, the biology of fish and associated fauna, and other related limnological matters.
6.	Public appreciation of natural history values must be developed through provision of nature trails, nature museums, nature guides, leaflets, lectures, and other interpretative activities. Data essential to such interpretative programs should be developed by well-planned research.
7.	The National Parks Service is responsible for management of wildlife in parks and interpretation to the public of the natural features (including wildlife) within parks. The Canadian Wildlife Service is responsible for research aimed at obtaining information needed for the management of wildlife in parks.
Territorial Wildlife General Policy
1.	The federal responsibility for Territorial wildlife is to provide research support for management and such management services as may be agreed upon between the Federal and Territorial governments, except that there is complete federal responsibility for migratory birds. There is also a residual authority that may be exercised to safeguard species in danger of extinction.
2.	Wildlife management in the Territories should be developed to and maintained at a level commensurate with the importance of the resource. Wildlife is one of the most important resources of the Territories, many of the inhabitants still depending in large measure upon wildlife for food and clothing. As the economy of the North develops, the importance of wildlife will change, but it will not diminish. The North will remain one of the few regions in the world where use of the land by wildlife will not be in serious competition with other uses. A continuing development of recreational use of wildlife is foreseen.
3.	A primary objective of wildlife management in the Territories is to prevent the population of any species from declining to a level from which it might not recover.
4.	Wildlife in the Territories should be managed so as to provide a sustained yield of those species that contribute to the subsistence of native populations. So long as native populations subsist in whole or in part on wildlife populations, this objective is secondary only to that of preventing the extinction of species.
5.	Wildlife may also provide a basis for recreation, and, consequently, contribute to the economy of Territorial residents. Management for recreational use may be harmonized with subsistence needs under certain circumstances.
Territorial Wildlife Research
1.	In line with the objectives of management, wildlife research in the Territories is aimed at determining the status of wildlife populations on a continuing basis, finding out what factors cause changes in the size and distribution of populations, and devising methods for maintaining desired populations.
2.	The status of populations will be determined by inventories and periodic censuses of acceptable design. Studies of reproductive success and the effective rate of recruitment to wildlife populations as indicated by observations of sex and age classes within populations also contribute to that end and may, in some instances, provide a more economic means of obtaining the necessary information. Studies of physiological condition can provide indicators of trends in wildlife populations.
3.	Management requires an understanding of the factors affecting changes in status and distribution of populations, as well as an awareness of such changes. Studies of condition and extent of range or habitat are important, particularly in areas where habitat conditions are amenable to modification, by control of forest fires, for example. Studies of mortality factors are also of high priority. These include hunting, the incidence and pathological effects of diseases and parasites, predation, and unusual weather conditions.
4.	Research provides the means for assessment of the effects of management as well as the information required to devise the methods of management. Studies must be directed toward determining the effects on wildlife and the users of wildlife of changes in regulations governing the harvest.
5.	Practical methods of disease prevention and control require continuing research and development.

Co-ordination
1.	Opportunities will be sought to promote inter-governmental consultation on the effects on wildlife of programs and projects that substantially alter the natural environment.
2.	Existing arrangements for consultation and co-ordination among agencies of the Federal Government will be reviewed and improved as necessary.
Consultation between governments and among government agencies is of particular importance in regard to wildlife. There are two reasons for this. For one thing, many
forms of wildlife are mobile and regularly cross boundaries between jurisdictions. Therefore, what is done in one area may affect wildlife in another area as well. The second point is that wildlife exists on lands used for a variety of purposes and controlled or influenced to some degree by a multitude of government agencies at both provincial and federal levels, and any major change in land use has some effect on the numbers and distribution of wildlife. Good wildlife management will not be achieved unless there is consultation and agreement during the planning phases of projects affecting land use and programs of broad biological impact.
